topics.title: Introduction to Rapid Response
topics.subtitle: Acute deterioration, bedside assessment, vitals, first pass stabilization

sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC (up to 60 L/min, FiO2 up to 100%) → NIPPV → intubation
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; ↓BP, then tension PTX, PE, or cardiogenic shock
Put on cardiac monitor

sections.title: Before You Arrive
items: On phone, first ask: current vitals, O2 need, mentation change, urine output, & any new chest pain, dyspnea, or bleeding.
If unstable, tell nursing to call rapid now, get full vitals, place oxygen, & confirm IV access while you head in.
If not crashing, give immediate low-risk orders: repeat vitals, fingerstick glucose, fix bad pulse ox waveform, ECG if needed, & stay at bedside if pt worsens.

sections.title: Immediate Bedside Priorities
items: Start with a doorway 10-second scan: are they talking, working to breathe, pale/diaphoretic/cyanotic, & what oxygen, monitors, drips, or pressors are already running?
If they look like they may crash, grab help now & start ABCs from room.
check airway, breathing, circulation, & mentation on arrival.
Get your own full vitals; place on telemetry & pulse oximetry if not already monitored.
Get EKG when chest pain, arrhythmia, syncope, unexplained ↓ BP, or ischemia is suspected
Confirm code status, allergies, IV access, oxygen delivery device, & whether pt is worsening or transiently abnormal.
Start time-sensitive treatment now for obvious instability while another team member gathers chart history & recent data

pairs.value: Know why pt is in hospital & what problems have already been identified.
Ask what triggered call now, what nurse thinks problem is, & what change happened over last few hours.
Look for baseline cardiopulmonary disease, renal failure, liver disease, endocrine disease, anticoagulation use, seizure history, & prior ICU admissions.
Review CBC, BMP/CMP, lactate, blood gas, troponin, BNP, cultures, glucose, & any changing values.
Identify what pt is actively receiving including fluids, antibiotics, anticoagulants, insulin, sedatives, opioids, & vasoactive medications.
Ask which important medications have been held such as beta blockers, antihypertensives, anticoagulants, steroids, diuretics, antiseizure drugs, or home oxygen support.
Clarify what changed today: procedure, dialysis, new medication, bleeding, aspiration, fever, rhythm change, seizure, fall, or worsening urine output.
Mentally upgrade pts who are recent ICU downgrades, septic, neutropenic, high risk postop, or recently bleeding.
Talking normally suggests a patent airway. Hoarseness, gurgling, stridor, snoring, or inability to clear secretions means airway threat. Use jaw thrust, suction, sit upright, & escalate early.
Count RR yourself, check WOB, wheeze/crackles/absent sounds, verify SpO2 waveform, & check oxygen setup. Escalate for marked tachypnea, hypoxemia despite support, or fatigue.
Feel pulse, repeat BP if it does not fit picture, check perfusion, review urine output, & look at access. Consider ECG, fingerstick glucose, & targeted labs early.
Check AVPU, orientation, pupils, speech, & gross motor function. Review for opioids, sedatives, insulin, seizure risk, or stroke symptoms.
Look for bleeding, rash, swelling, distended abdomen, surgical complications, line problems, or obvious bedside clues.

sections.title: Focused Exam / ROS
items: Do a focused physical exam directed by instability: mentation, speech, WOB, lung exam, cardiac rhythm, perfusion, abdomen, edema, bleeding, & skin findings.
If pt can answer questions, get brief ROS for chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, dizziness, headache, focal deficit, fever, abdominal pain, & bleeding symptoms.
Use bedside nurse's observations when pt cannot provide history: last known well, urine output, mentation trend, O2 need, & symptom progression.

sections.title: Typical Team Composition
items: Bedside nurse & charge nurse
Primary team clinician or covering provider
Rapid response nurse
Respiratory therapist when respiratory distress, hypoxemia, or airway concern
Pharmacist when medication support, pressors, reversal agents, or emergent dosing is needed
More support as needed: ICU team, anesthesia, security, or procedural staff

sections.title: Why Rapid Response Is Called
items: Acute AMS, WOB, oxygenation, heart rate, BP, or perfusion
Concern from bedside staff that pt is decompensating, even if trigger does not fit strict threshold
New chest pain, syncope, seizure, severe agitation, suspected stroke, sepsis, or unexpected bleeding
Any situation where early team-based assessment may prevent cardiac arrest or unplanned ICU transfer

sections.title: Escalation Lane
items: Wardmanageable: problem identified, initial treatment started, repeat vitals improving, & monitoring plan is clear.
Urgent help: call senior, ICU, specialty, or procedural support early if pt is high risk or may need a higher level of care.
Rapid / code now: severe airway threat, major respiratory distress, shock, severe dysrhythmia,worsening mentation, or any pt who looks close to arrest.

sections.title: Assessment & Initial Workup
items: Generate practical differential diagnosis based on first minute of information,then narrow it with the exam, vitals, ECG, & targeted testing.
Order appropriate labs & imaging early when they will change management: CBC, CMP, VBG/ABG, lactate, troponin, BNP, cultures, chest xray, CT, or POCUS as needed.

Treat now reversible problems without waiting for every result: oxygen, suction, bronchodilators, fluids, vasopressors, glucose, naloxone, antibiotics, blood products, or antiarrhythmics as clinically indicated.
Escalate to ICU, anesthesia, cath lab, stroke pathway, code team, or surgical consultation when bedside trajectory suggests pt may not remain stable on floor.

topics.title: Breaking Bad News & Family Communication
topics.subtitle: Structured framework for delivering serious news — preparation, conversation, and follow-up

sections.title: Overview
items: Communication with patients and families should be part of ongoing care — at regular intervals and whenever the clinical situation changes
Given the severity of illness in critically ill patients, breaking bad news is a common occurrence during and after rapid responses
Where possible, this should be led by a senior clinician — but the pace of deterioration may not allow that
What follows is a structured template adaptable to most situations; individual circumstances and the people involved will require flexibility

sections.title: Preparation
items: Confirm you have the right patient — review the latest details on their condition, recent changes, and the current management plan before the conversation
Find a private space: quiet room or pulled curtains — privacy reduces distress and allows the family to respond freely
Minimize interruptions: hand pagers and phones to a colleague when possible; this conversation deserves undivided attention
Have the patient's nurse present — continuity of information and support for the family after you leave
Introduce yourself clearly (name, role, relationship to the patient's care) and confirm who you are speaking with and their relationship to the patient
Sit at the same level as the person you are speaking to — avoid standing over them; maintain comfortable eye contact

pairs.key: Step 1 — What do they already know?
pairs.value: Ask what information has already been given: 'What has the team told you so far about how things are going?' Confirm their understanding — families often receive fragmented or inconsistent information

pairs.key: Step 2 — What do they want to know?
pairs.value: Ask what they want to hear: 'Is there anything specific you'd like me to explain?' Some want a full overview; others want to ask one question at a time — follow their lead

Prepare them before delivering bad news: 'I'm afraid I have some difficult news' or 'I want to be honest with you — the situation is very serious.' This gives them a moment to brace emotionally before the detail

pairs.key: Step 4 — Allow them to pause or decline
pairs.value: Some families may not be ready to hear more right now — that is okay. Let them know: 'You do not have to hear all of this at once — I am here when you are ready.' Note: a family member cannot refuse information on behalf of a patient who has decision-making capacity

Explain the clinical situation clearly and honestly. Use plain language; avoid medical jargon or translate it. Use words like 'dying' or 'death' when appropriate — euphemisms can create ambiguity. Do not give false reassurance. If you do not know the answer, say so
Re-state key points and confirm they landed: 'Does that make sense?' or 'Can you tell me what you are taking away from this?' Silence after bad news is normal — sit with it

Ask: 'Is there anything on your mind you'd like to talk about?' Their agenda may differ from yours — a family member may be preoccupied with a practical issue, a prior interaction, or a specific fear; listen without rushing

'How does that leave you feeling?' or 'This must be incredibly hard to hear.' Acknowledging emotions is therapeutic in itself — do not redirect to clinical facts when someone is expressing grief, fear, or anger

pairs.key: Step 9 — Summarize and explain the plan
pairs.value: Recap what was discussed and outline what happens next — diagnostics, treatments, comfort measures, or further conversations. Make the plan feel concrete even when uncertainty remains
Make clear that you or a team member is available: 'Please ask the nurse to reach us if questions come up.' Identify who the family's main point of contact will be going forward
Write a note in the medical record summarizing: who was present, key information shared, family understanding, concerns raised, and the plan — this ensures continuity across the team

sections.title: Language Tips
items: Use plain language: 'the heart is not pumping well' instead of 'cardiogenic shock'
Use direct words when appropriate: 'dying' and 'death' are clearer than 'passing' or 'not doing well'
Avoid information overload — one clear concept at a time; pause and check in frequently
Avoid false reassurance: 'We are doing everything we can' is okay — 'I am sure things will get better' is not
It is appropriate and honest to say: 'I do not know' or 'We are not sure yet — here is what we do know'
Silence is not failure — sitting quietly after difficult news gives the family space to process

pairs.value: Early in any serious admission or rapid deterioration — ideally before a crisis forces the discussion. Do not wait until the patient is peri-arrest to address code status and goals

'What matters most to your family member?' and 'What would they consider a good quality of life?' — not just 'Do you want us to do everything?' The latter puts families in a position of guilt rather than guidance

If the patient has capacity, they direct their own care — a family member cannot override this. If the patient lacks capacity, identify the legal surrogate and clarify their role: substituted judgment (what the patient would want), not substituted preference (what the family wants)

Describe what CPR actually involves — realistic description of resuscitation, survival rates in the clinical context, and what life may look like afterward. Families often agree to DNR when they understand what they are and are not declining

Frame comfort care as active, not passive: 'We will continue to treat pain, shortness of breath, and anxiety aggressively — we are not giving up, we are changing our focus to what matters most to the patient'

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Communication is a process — it may take several conversations before a serious situation is fully understood and accepted
Families may be angry — about the diagnosis, prior care, or the situation itself; acknowledge the anger, do not dismiss it, and do not criticize previous management
Do not deliver news in a hallway, in front of other patients, or while holding a pager — environment matters
Do not use jargon or acronyms without explaining them (ICU, DNR, ARDS, etc.)
Do not overload — too much information at once reduces retention; focus on the 2–3 most important points
Do not leave without a clear next step — families should always know who to call and what to expect next
An apology for a difficult situation ('I am so sorry this is happening') is not an admission of fault — it is human and appropriate
